chunks: "I protect against these because every part has a limit, and real systems regularly leave the nominal range.
Overcurrent, usually a short or a stalled motor, is a heat problem: power is I to the 2R , so ten times the current is a hundred times the heating.
Traces fuse, connectors melt, batteries vent.
Overvoltage is a breakdown problem: gate oxides, capacitor dielectrics and junctions have a hard limit, so a spike or the wrong adapter can permanently kill a part, often silently.
Undervoltage is a function problem: a microcontroller below its minimum supply can execute garbage, corrupt flash, and a FET with too little gate drive sits half on and cooks itself.
So I'd layer it. At the input: a fuse or eFuse, a TVS for spikes, reverse-polarity protection. At the regulator: current limit, thermal shutdown, and overvoltage protection.
At the system level: a supervisor or brown-out reset and undervoltage lockout so the system only runs when the rails are good.
And in software, fault flags so the system can degrade gracefully instead of just dying.
What I'd pick depends on cost, the consequence of failure, and whether the fault is a one-off or repetitive.
A hobby LED board gets a resistor; a battery pack gets redundant protection."
